summary: Qatar is a peninsular country in the east of the Arabian Peninsula with abundant natural gas resources and one of the highest per capita incomes in the world; it hosted the 2022 FIFA World Cup.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam reached the Qatar peninsula in the 7th century. In the 18th century the Al Thani family moved in from Najd, following Wahhabi Sunni Islam, ruled Qatar from 1878, and after independence in 1971 made Islam the state religion and Islamic law the main source of legislation. Qatari citizens are almost all Muslim, mostly Sunni with Shia about one tenth; among foreign residents there are also many Muslims from South Asia, the Middle East and North Africa. Because the foreign population makes up about ninety percent, Muslims account for about two thirds of the total population.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Qatar's Christians are almost all foreign workers, mainly from the Philippines, Kerala in India, Lebanon, Europe and America, who arrived in large numbers after the oil boom of the 1970s and the gas boom of the 2000s. In 2008 the Qatari government allocated land on the outskirts of Doha for a 'Religious Complex', where the first Catholic church, Our Lady of the Rosary, was built, and Catholic, Anglican, Orthodox and other churches are concentrated there.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: Hindus are mainly foreign workers from India and Nepal, who came to Qatar in large numbers after the 2000s with Qatar's gas industry, infrastructure and the construction projects for the 2022 World Cup. Because Qatar does not permit the building of Hindu temples, believers mostly practice their religion in private places.

ranking.name: Buddhism
ranking.description: Buddhists are mainly foreign workers and professionals from Sri Lanka, Thailand, Nepal and East Asia; their numbers are small, and they mainly hold activities in private places.

religion.background: The Qatar peninsula accepted Islam in the 7th century and traditionally lived by pearl diving and nomadism. The Al Thani family moved in during the 18th century and established its rule in the 19th century, following Wahhabi Islam. After independence in 1971 Islam became the state religion. After the discovery of oil in the 1940s and, in 1971, of the North Field, the world's largest natural gas field, large numbers of foreign workers flooded in, so that the foreign population makes up about ninety percent, bringing Christianity, Hinduism and Buddhism.

language.official: Arabic is the official language, and English is widely used in business.

ranking.name: Arabic
ranking.description: Arabic is the mother tongue of Qatari citizens and belongs to the Gulf Arabic dialects, close to the dialects of the east of the Arabian Peninsula. In 2019 Qatar passed a law requiring that government agencies, public schools and official documents use Arabic, in order to protect national identity. Because Qatari citizens make up only about one tenth of the total population, and there are also Arab foreign workers from Egypt, Jordan, Syria and elsewhere, Arabic speakers make up about forty percent.

ranking.name: Nepali
ranking.description: Nepali is spoken by the many foreign workers from Nepal, who arrived in large numbers after the 2000s with Qatar's construction boom, especially after Qatar won the right to host the 2022 World Cup in 2010, when building stadiums, a metro and hotels required large numbers of workers. The working and living conditions of Nepali workers have drawn the attention of international human rights organizations.

ranking.name: Bengali
ranking.description: Bengali is spoken by foreign workers from Bangladesh, who work mainly in construction, cleaning and services. Bangladesh has exported labor to the Gulf states since the 1970s, and remittances from abroad are an important pillar of the Bangladeshi economy.

ranking.name: Malayalam
ranking.description: Malayalam is the language of the state of Kerala in southern India. Kerala and the Gulf region have been in contact through trade across the Arabian Sea since ancient times, and after the oil boom of the 1970s large numbers of Keralites went to Qatar to work in retail, healthcare, engineering and services, forming a huge community.

language.history: Gulf Arabic dialects have long been in common use in Qatar, and the coastal society, based mainly on pearl diving, had close contacts with India and Persia, so the vocabulary contains quite a few Persian and Indian loanwords. During the British protectorate of 1916–1971, English became the language of external relations and commerce. After independence in 1971 Arabic became the official language, but the oil and gas economy brought large numbers of foreign workers, and English became the common language among different groups; in 2019 Qatar legislated to strengthen the use of Arabic.

ranking.name: Machboos
ranking.description: Rice is cooked together with chicken or lamb stewed with cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, dried black lime and baharat spice blend, the rice absorbing the meat juices and turning golden in color.
ranking.history: Machboos is a traditional Gulf dish whose spices and method are deeply influenced by Indian Ocean trade. Before oil was discovered, Qatar's economy was based mainly on pearl diving, and pearl merchants had close trade with India and Persia, bringing back rice, spices and the cooking method of Indian biryani. It is the staple of Qatari family lunches and an essential dish for entertaining guests at weddings and festivals.

ranking.name: Harees
ranking.description: Wheat grains are stewed with chicken or lamb for a long time and then repeatedly beaten into a thick porridge, seasoned with ghee and cinnamon, with a creamy texture.
ranking.history: Harees is one of the oldest dishes of the Arabian Peninsula, already recorded in 10th-century Baghdad cookbooks. In Qatar it is closely tied to Islamic religious festivals, and during Ramadan it is an essential dish for the iftar meal, with families also sharing harees with neighbors and the poor. It is also common at Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, symbolizing sharing and reunion.

ranking.name: Luqaimat
ranking.description: A yeast-fermented batter is spooned into hot oil and fried into small balls, golden and crisp outside and soft inside, drizzled with date syrup and sprinkled with sesame seeds.
ranking.history: Luqaimat is already recorded in 13th-century Abbasid cookbooks of Baghdad, and its name means 'small bites'. It has been passed down in the Gulf region for hundreds of years, and because dates are the most important crop of the Arabian Peninsula, seasoning with date syrup is a local specialty. In Qatar it is the most popular dessert for breaking the fast during Ramadan, and every household makes it.

ranking.name: Thareed
ranking.description: Local thin bread (regag) is torn up and spread on the bottom of a plate, then drenched with a thick stew of lamb, potatoes, pumpkin, tomatoes and spices, letting the bread soak up the broth.
ranking.history: Thareed is one of the oldest dishes of the Arabian Peninsula; according to the Hadith, the Prophet Muhammad loved this dish very much and once used it as a metaphor for the best of all foods. Because of its association with the Prophet, it is especially popular during Ramadan and is a traditional iftar dish in Qatari homes. It also reflects the Bedouin ingenuity of combining bread with stew to save food.

ranking.name: Balaleet
ranking.description: Thin vermicelli noodles are sautéed sweet with sugar, cardamom, saffron and rose water and covered with a thin omelet, being both savory and sweet, often eaten as breakfast on festive mornings.
ranking.history: Balaleet is a traditional Gulf breakfast, and the use of vermicelli reflects the trade exchanges between the Arabian Peninsula and Persia and India, while the saffron and rose water mostly came from Persia. In Qatar it is often a weekend breakfast or a dish for festival mornings, especially on the morning of Eid al-Fitr, when family members enjoy this dish of blended sweet and savory together.
